output.question: How is revenue defined in the primer?
output.answer:

> For a single product, revenue equals the selling price multiplied by the number of units sold. [S1]
output.reference_answer: Revenue is the money a business takes in from sales before any costs are deducted; for a single product it equals selling price times units sold.

output.question: What is the difference between a percentage-point change and a percent change?
output.answer:
From your course materials (quoted directly):

> A percentage-point change is the simple difference between two percentages: a conversion rate that rises from 2% to 3% has increased by 1 percentage point. [S1]

> A percent change is the difference relative to the starting value: the same move from 2% to 3% is a 50% increase. [S1]

> Reports should state which measure they use, because confusing the two can make a small change look large or a large change look small. [S1]

> When a rate changes, there are two different ways to describe the change. [S1]
output.reference_answer: A percentage-point change is the simple difference between two percentages; a percent change is that difference relative to the starting value (2% to 3% is +1 point but a 50% increase).
cited_contexts: When a rate changes, there are two different ways to describe the change. A percentage-point change is the simple difference between two percentages: a conversion rate that rises from 2% to 3% has increased by 1 percentage point. A percent change is the difference relative to the starting value: the same move from 2% to 3% is a 50% increase. Reports should state which measure they use, because confusing the two can make a small change look large or a large change look small.

output.question: What are some examples of variable costs?
output.answer:
From your course materials (quoted directly):

> Variable costs change in proportion to the number of units sold, for example materials, packaging, payment fees and delivery. [S1]

> Example: a workshop with a variable cost of ₹300 and an average total cost of ₹380 per unit (including allocated rent) receives a one-off order for 100 units at ₹340 each. [S2]

> Fixed costs, such as rent and salaried staff, do not change with short-run volume. [S1]
output.reference_answer: Materials, packaging, payment fees and delivery.
cited_contexts: Variable costs change in proportion to the number of units sold, for example materials, packaging, payment fees and delivery. Fixed costs, such as rent and salaried staff, do not change with short-run volume. Separating the two is the first step in understanding how a decision affects profit.

For decisions about one additional order, what matters is the marginal (incremental) cost of serving it, usually the variable cost, not the average total cost per unit, which includes fixed costs that will be paid anyway. Example: a workshop with a variable cost of ₹300 and an average total cost of ₹380 per unit (including allocated rent) receives a one-off order for 100 units at ₹340 each. If spare capacity exists and fixed costs will not change, the order adds (340 − 300) × 100 = ₹4,000 of contribution, even though ₹340 is below the average total cost.

output.question: What is the contribution margin ratio of a product priced at ₹500 with a variable cost of ₹300?
output.answer:
From your course materials (quoted directly):

> Example: a product sells for ₹500 and has a variable cost of ₹300 per unit. [S1]

> Speaker notes for slide 4 (Contribution Margin): For a ₹1,200 jacket with an ₹800 variable cost, contribution per unit is ₹400 and the contribution margin ratio is one third. [S2]
output.reference_answer: 40% (contribution of ₹200 divided by the ₹500 price).
cited_contexts:
Contribution margin per unit is the selling price minus the variable cost per unit. It is the amount each additional unit contributes towards covering fixed costs and then generating profit. Total contribution equals the contribution margin per unit multiplied by the number of units sold. The contribution margin ratio expresses contribution as a share of the selling price.
Contribution margin per unit = price − variable cost per unit
Contribution margin ratio = (price − variable cost) ÷ price
Example: a product sells for ₹500 and has a variable cost of ₹300 per unit. Its contribution margin per unit is ₹200 and its contribution margin ratio is 40%.
Speaker notes for slide 4 (Contribution Margin): For a ₹1,200 jacket with an ₹800 variable cost, contribution per unit is ₹400 and the contribution margin ratio is one third.

Break-even volume is the number of units at which total contribution exactly covers fixed costs. With fixed costs of ₹60,000 and contribution per unit of ₹200, the business must sell 300 units to break even.
Break-even volume = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit

output.question: Why does a randomised A/B test help establish a causal effect?
output.answer:
From your course materials (quoted directly):

> A randomised controlled experiment, often called an A/B test, assigns customers to groups at random so that confounders are balanced on average. [S1]

> A randomized experiment with a control group is the cleanest way to measure the causal effect. [S2]

> Incrementality tests, which compare exposed and unexposed groups, give a better estimate of the causal effect. [S3]
output.reference_answer: Random assignment balances confounders on average, so differences between groups can be attributed to the treatment within sampling error.
cited_contexts: A randomised controlled experiment, often called an A/B test, assigns customers to groups at random so that confounders are balanced on average. If the treated group then behaves differently from the control group, the difference can be attributed to the treatment, within the limits of sampling error.

Customer lifetime value (CLV) estimates the total contribution a customer generates over their relationship with the business. A simple version multiplies the average monthly contribution per customer by the expected customer lifetime in months. Using revenue instead of contribution overstates CLV, because it ignores the cost of serving the customer. For example, a customer who pays ₹500 per month at a 40% contribution margin ratio generates ₹200 of contribution per month; with an expected lifetime of 18 months, CLV is ₹3,600.
CLV = average monthly contribution per customer × expected lifetime in months

40 rupees with a variable cost of 25 rupees. Each pod contributes 15 rupees. Now the marketing team proposes cutting the price to 35 rupees. The variable cost does not change, so the contribution per pod falls from 15 rupees to 10 rupees. A 12 and a half percent price cut has removed one-third of the contribution per unit. A price cut reduces the contribution of every unit sold, not just the revenue. Because variable costs stay the same, the contribution per unit falls by the full amount of the price cut. To keep total contribution unchanged, volume must rise by the ratio of the old to the new contribution per unit.
Required volume increase = (old contribution per unit ÷ new contribution per unit) − 1
Continuing the example, cutting the price from ₹500 to ₹450 lowers contribution per unit from ₹200 to ₹150. Volume must rise by 200 ÷ 150 − 1 = 33.3% just to earn the same total contribution. Keeping revenue constant would need only an 11.1% increase (500 ÷ 450 − 1), which is why plans that aim to 'make up the revenue' can still leave the business with less contribution to cover its fixed costs.
Preserving revenue and preserving contribution are different goals. Revenue preservation ignores variable costs; contribution preservation accounts for them.
